Optimizing Network Performance and Cost
Practical patterns to reduce egress charges, keep traffic private, and improve global user latency.
In this lesson

You will learn data transfer pricing drivers, when to use VPC Endpoints, NAT Gateway vs NAT instance trade-offs, Global Accelerator benefits, and how to design a cost-aware network.

Why this matters
Egress charges and latency are recurring operational costs. Optimizing them lowers bills and improves user experience.
Explore Key Topics

VPC Endpoints

screens.title: Data Transfer Costs — Where and why they apply
screens.narratorSegment: Data transfer costs are charges for moving data between locations: within AZs, across AZs, between regions, and to or from the internet. The most important practical rule is that keeping related resources in the same Availability Zone or at least the same region minimizes charges. For example, two EC2 instances in the same AZ usually exchange data at no charge, while moving traffic between AZs in the same region typically incurs a small fee. Cross-region transfers are significantly more expensive and should be avoided for high-volume flows. Another common source of egress is when instances access services via an Internet Gateway or NAT — traffic leaving the AWS network to the public internet can incur per-GB costs. Caching using CloudFront reduces origin pulls and therefore origin egress charges for public content. A common misconception is that cloud traffic is always cheap; in reality, seemingly small design choices, like placing database replicas in another region, can create large recurring bills. Takeaway: map your traffic flows, label high-volume paths, and prioritize co-location or caching before accepting cross-region or internet egress. Data Transfer Costs — Where and why they apply means minimize cross-az, cross-region, and internet egress by co-locating resources or using caching and private paths.. In practical terms, understand the billing boundaries that affect your architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Minimize cross-AZ, cross-region, and internet egress by co-locating resources or using caching and private paths.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Data Transfer Costs — Where and why they apply
Definition and rules
  • Same AZ traffic is typically free; cross-AZ traffic usually costs a small per-GB fee.
  • Cross-region transfer is expensive; avoid moving large datasets between regions.
  • Internet egress from AWS to the public internet incurs per-GB charges.
  • CloudFront caching reduces repeated origin egress by serving cached objects close to users.
Example
If a processing pipeline downloads 5 TB daily from S3, using an S3 Gateway Endpoint keeps that traffic inside the region and avoids internet egress charges that would apply if accessed through a NAT or Internet Gateway.
Diagram substitute: Traffic map
High-volume flows: tag them. Place compute and storage in the same AZ or region. If cross-region is required, compress or reduce transfers and cache responses.
Key Takeaway

Label and minimize high-volume network flows first; co-location and caching are the cheapest optimizations.

screens.title: VPC Endpoints — Private connectivity without the internet
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Endpoints provide private, secure connectivity between your VPC and supported AWS services without traversing the public internet. There are two kinds you must know. Gateway endpoints are specific to S3 and DynamoDB. They act as a route table entry that directs traffic for those services to an internal gateway; importantly they are free to use, and they remove internet exposure for those service calls. Interface endpoints are powered by PrivateLink and create Elastic Network Interfaces with private IPs in your subnets. Use interface endpoints when a service supports PrivateLink or when you need private connectivity to many services such as SQS, SNS, Kinesis, or custom endpoints for your own services. A practical example: an EC2 worker in a private subnet that reads and writes lots of S3 data should use an S3 Gateway Endpoint to avoid egress charges. A frequent misconception is that interface endpoints are free; while they improve security they incur hourly and per-GB costs, so choose the endpoint type based on service and traffic volume. Final thought: design endpoints early for storage-heavy or chatty service traffic to avoid retrofitting expensive network paths.

keyIdea.title: VPC Endpoints
keyIdea.text: Gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB (free); interface endpoints via PrivateLink for many other services (ENI-based).

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › VPC Endpoints — Private connectivity without the internet
Interface vs Gateway
  • Gateway Endpoint: route table entry, S3 and DynamoDB only, free to use.
  • Interface Endpoint: PrivateLink-powered ENIs, supports many services, incurs costs.
Concrete example
An analytics cluster that repeatedly reads S3 data should use an S3 Gateway Endpoint so reads stay within the region and avoid NAT or internet egress.
Decision guide
  1. Is the target service S3 or DynamoDB? Use a Gateway Endpoint.
  2. Does the service support PrivateLink or require an ENI? Use an Interface Endpoint.
  3. Estimate traffic: high-volume storage flows favor gateway endpoints where possible.
Common mistake
Assuming all endpoints are free. Interface endpoints can add per-hour and per-GB charges, so confirm costs before wide deployment.

screens.title: NAT Gateway vs NAT Instance
screens.narratorSegment: When private instances need to initiate outbound internet connections, you have two main choices: a managed NAT Gateway or a self-managed NAT instance. NAT Gateway is a fully managed AWS service. It scales automatically within an Availability Zone and requires no OS-level maintenance. For production workloads where uptime and simplicity matter, a NAT Gateway is the preferred option despite per-hour and per-GB charges. A NAT instance, by contrast, is a regular EC2 instance running NAT software. It can be cheaper for extremely low-volume traffic and gives control over software and metrics, but it adds operational burden: you must handle patching, scaling, failover, and monitoring. For high-throughput or important services, the management overhead of NAT instances typically outweighs savings. A common misconception is that NAT instances always save money — if traffic volume grows, manual scaling and NAT instance failure can cause outages and hidden costs. Practical advice: estimate expected data processed through the NAT; if it is large or variable, choose NAT Gateway and focus on reducing traffic through private endpoints instead of relying on egress. NAT Gateway vs NAT Instance means nat gateway for reliability and low ops; nat instance for low-volume, tightly controlled scenarios where you accept management overhead.. In practical terms, trade-offs in cost, availability, and operational overhead. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › NAT Gateway vs NAT Instance
NAT Gateway (Managed)
  • Fully managed, AZ-level high availability when deployed per-AZ.
  • Auto-scaling for bandwidth; no patching or OS maintenance required.
  • Charges: hourly + per-GB processed.
Preferred for production and variable traffic.
NAT Instance (Self-managed)
  • EC2 instance running NAT software; offers full administrative control.
  • Potentially lower cost at very low throughput, but needs patching and HA design.
  • Requires Auto Scaling or scripts for failover, adding operational risk.
Suitable for constrained, low-traffic, or experimental setups where you accept the overhead.
Decision checklist
Estimate GB/month
Assess operational capacity
Plan HA per AZ

screens.title: AWS Global Accelerator
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Global Accelerator provides two static Anycast IP addresses that serve as fixed entry points for your global users. User traffic goes to the closest AWS edge location by Anycast and then traverses the optimized AWS backbone to your application endpoints, such as load balancers or EC2 instances. This reduces latency compared with relying solely on the public internet and improves availability because Global Accelerator monitors endpoint health and fails over to the next healthy endpoint automatically. Use Global Accelerator when you have a global user base sensitive to latency or when consistent performance and quick failover are business requirements. A practical example: a web application with users across continents can route users to nearest edges and then across AWS network to the origin region, achieving large latency reduction. A common misconception is that Global Accelerator replaces CDN for static content; it does not cache content. Instead, pair CloudFront for caching with Global Accelerator for optimal routing of dynamic or TCP flows. Final question to reflect on: are your users globally distributed enough that round-trip time gains justify the service cost?

keyIdea.text: Static Anycast IPs and optimized routing across AWS backbone reduce latency and provide rapid failover for global apps.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › AWS Global Accelerator
What it provides
  • Two static Anycast IP addresses as fixed entry points.
  • Routing to the nearest edge and across AWS backbone to endpoints.
  • Automatic failover between healthy endpoints.
Example
A global application routes users to the nearest edge; traffic then travels the AWS backbone to the primary region, saving significant latency versus internet-only paths.
When to use
Use Global Accelerator when global latency matters, when you need static IPs for clients, and when faster failover improves availability. Pair with CloudFront for caching static assets.
Misconception check
Global Accelerator is not a caching layer. Use CloudFront for caching and Global Accelerator to optimize routing of dynamic or non-HTTP flows.

screens.title: Egress-Only Internet Gateway for IPv6
screens.narratorSegment: For IPv6-only subnets that require outbound internet access but must remain unreachable from the internet, the Egress-Only Internet Gateway is the proper tool. It functions like NAT for IPv6: it allows instances to initiate outbound connections while preventing inbound connections initiated from the internet. This preserves security for IPv6 resources that should not be publicly addressable while still enabling package updates or external A P I calls. A practical scenario: if you run IPv6-only compute that needs to fetch updates but must not accept inbound traffic, an Egress-Only Internet Gateway meets the requirement without resorting to IPv4 NAT. A common misconception is that traditional NAT Gateway covers IPv6; NAT Gateway is an IPv4 construct. The takeaway is to select the right mechanism for the IP family in use and to validate that route tables for IPv6 route outbound traffic through the egress-only gateway. Always verify endpoint reachability after configuration to ensure no unintended inbound exposure. Egress-Only Internet Gateway for IPv6 means egress-only internet gateway allows outbound ipv6 connections while preventing inbound internet initiation.. In practical terms, ipv6 outbound-only internet access without inbound reachability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Egress-Only Internet Gateway for IPv6
Concept
Egress-Only Internet Gateway enables outbound IPv6 from private subnets while blocking inbound connections initiated from the internet. It fills the IPv6 gap where NAT is not applicable.
Quick validation
After adding the gateway to your VPC and route table, verify outbound connectivity and ensure no open inbound ports appear in security scans.
Why it matters
It gives IPv6-only workloads safe outbound access without exposing them to inbound internet connections, maintaining the principle of least privilege.
Misconception
Do not assume NAT applies to IPv6. Use the egress-only gateway for IPv6 outbound-only needs.

screens.title: Hands-on: Provision NAT Gateway and S3 Gateway Endpoint (CLI)
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll step through the starter CLI commands that set up a NAT Gateway, update a private route table, and create an S3 Gateway Endpoint. Follow the commands as a sequence of discrete steps you can reproduce. First allocate an Elastic IP and create the NAT Gateway in your public subnet; the NAT Gateway requires the Elastic IP and will be assigned a resource ID. Next, update the private route table so that 0.0.0.0/0 points to the NAT Gateway — this gives private instances outbound internet access through the managed gateway. Then create a VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3 and attach it to the private route table; this ensures S3 traffic uses the internal gateway and avoids internet egress. In a lab, you would then launch an EC2 instance into the private subnet and verify connectivity by pinging a public IP and running an S3 list. Remember to wait for the NAT Gateway to reach available state before creating routes. This sequence reproduces the scenario safely and is the baseline for validating both internet and S3 access from private instances.

keyIdea.title: CLI flow
keyIdea.text: Allocate EIP → create NAT Gateway → add route to private table → create S3 Gateway Endpoint → verify from private instance.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Hands-on: Provision NAT Gateway and S3 Gateway Endpoint (CLI)
Starter commands
# Allocate an Elastic IP for the NAT Gateway
aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc

# Create a NAT Gateway in the public subnet
aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id subnet-pub123 --allocation-id eipalloc-0abcdef1234567890

# Update private route table to use the NAT Gateway
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-priv789 --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --nat-gateway-id nat-0fedcba9876543210

# Create an S3 Gateway Endpoint for the VPC
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-1234567890abcdef0 \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 \
  --vpc-endpoint-type Gateway \
  --route-table-ids rtb-priv789
Verification
From a private instance, verify internet and S3 access with package updates and an S3 list. Use a bastion host for SSH if needed.
Example checks
ping 8.8.8.8 -c 4, curl https://example.com, aws s3 ls — all should succeed from the private instance if routes are correct.
Wait note
NAT Gateway creation can take minutes. Wait for it to reach available state before creating routes to avoid transient failures.

screens.title: Lab Scenario: Step-by-step architecture
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through a small lab architecture you can deploy to validate behavior. Step one: create a public subnet for the NAT Gateway and a private subnet for your worker instances. Step two: allocate an Elastic IP and create a NAT Gateway in the public subnet; this gives private instances outbound internet access. Step three: update the private subnet's route table to send 0.0.0.0/0 through the NAT Gateway. Step four: create a Gateway Endpoint for S3 and attach it to the private route table so S3-bound traffic stays within the AWS network. Step five: launch an EC2 instance into the private subnet and SSH via a bastion host in the public subnet to perform verification commands. Because each step changes routing and potential egress, validate connectivity after each change. A common misunderstanding is to assume the S3 endpoint magically changes all routes — you must add the endpoint to the appropriate route table. The final takeaway: follow the sequence, verify after each step, and record where data flows to prove cost and security benefits. In practical terms, create public subnet, nat gateway, private subnet, and s3 endpoint. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. narration.text: This lesson walks through a small lab architecture you can deploy to validate behavior. Step one: create a public subnet for the NAT Gateway and a private subnet for your worker instances. Step two: allocate an Elastic IP and create a NAT Gateway in the public subnet; this gives private instances outbound internet access. Step three: update the private subnet's route table to send 0.0.0.0/0 through the NAT Gateway. Step four: create a Gateway Endpoint for S3 and attach it to the private route table so S3-bound traffic stays within the AWS network. Step five: launch an EC2 instance into the private subnet and SSH via a bastion host in the public subnet to perform verification commands. Because each step changes routing and potential egress, validate connectivity after each change. A common misunderstanding is to assume the S3 endpoint magically changes all routes — you must add the endpoint to the appropriate route table. The final takeaway: follow the sequence, verify after each step, and record where data flows to prove cost and security benefits. screens.title: Monitoring and cost controls
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring network traffic and cost is essential once you deploy optimizations. Use CloudWatch and VPC flow logs to see where traffic is flowing and tag high-volume flows. In parallel, set Cost Explorer alerts and budgets targeting data transfer categories so you get notified of unusual spikes. screens.title: Common mistakes and safe optimizations
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes lead to higher costs or security exposures. First, not using VPC Endpoints for S3/DynamoDB traffic causes that traffic to traverse internet gateways or NATs, which increases egress charges and exposure. Second, under-sizing NAT capacity or relying on a single NAT instance without HA causes performance bottlenecks or outages when traffic grows. Third, placing replicated backups or analytics nodes in a different region without compressing transfers can lead to unexpectedly large cross-region bills. To mitigate these, adopt safe optimizations: prefer gateway endpoints for storage-heavy flows, choose NAT Gateway when you need low ops and predictable scaling, and compress or schedule cross-region transfers during off-peak windows if they cannot be avoided. Also, balance security and cost — do not open S3 buckets to public access merely to avoid transfer complexity. The closing question to consider is: which of your current data flows would you first change to save cost without reducing security? Common mistakes and safe optimizations means avoid exposing storage to the internet to save costs; prefer private endpoints and managed nat for production.. In practical terms, avoid pitfalls that increase cost or weaken security. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Key Concepts

Third, choose NAT Gateway for production outbound needs because it reduces operational risk; use NAT instances only when traffic volumes are tiny and you accept the management overhead. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a practical understanding of how network design choices affect both performance and cost. You will learn what drives data transfer charges, when traffic stays free inside the AWS fabric, and how services like VPC Endpoints, NAT Gateway, and Global Accelerator help you optimize both latency and bills. We'll ground the ideas with concrete examples: keeping related compute and storage in the same Availability Zone to avoid cross-AZ fees, using an S3 Gateway Endpoint to remove internet egress for high-volume S3 transfers, and when Global Accelerator can justify its cost for global user bases. I'll also highlight common mistakes, like relying on internet gateways for internal service access or under-sizing NAT solutions, and offer a short checklist you can apply to your architectures. By the end, you'll be able to choose the right endpoint types, plan NAT strategy for private subnets, and decide when to use Global Accelerator for global performance gains. Consider: what network traffic in your environment currently creates the biggest cost?

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to make concrete, cost-aware network design decisions. First, you will learn to analyze how data transfer costs are incurred across Availability Zones and regions, and how simple placement choices reduce recurring egress fees. Second, you will be able to choose and configure the appropriate VPC Endpoint type for AWS services, understanding how interface endpoints differ from gateway endpoints and where each saves money and increases security. These are practical skills: for example, choosing an S3 Gateway Endpoint can remove egress for high-volume S3 access. You'll also be asked to evaluate NAT options and Global Accelerator based on traffic patterns and global latency. Each objective pairs a conceptual claim with a hands-on milestone so you can verify competency in real deployments. Keep in mind that cost optimization must never undermine security — secure private access often delivers both safety and savings.

This second objectives slide focuses on applying and validating the patterns. You will practice configuring route table entries for gateway endpoints, launching a NAT Gateway and updating private route tables, and verifying connectivity from a private instance. You'll also learn to interpret CloudWatch or Cost Explorer signals that indicate where egress charges accumulate, such as large cross-region transfers or unexpected internet-bound traffic. A key objective is to be able to recommend either a NAT Gateway or NAT instance with a clear rationale that balances operational overhead and expected throughput. Finally, you will learn when Global Accelerator should be proposed: specifically for applications with a global user base where latency reduction and static entry points are worth the service cost. Each objective ends with a verification step so you can prove the competency in a lab or real environment.

Data transfer costs are charges for moving data between locations: within AZs, across AZs, between regions, and to or from the internet. The most important practical rule is that keeping related resources in the same Availability Zone or at least the same region minimizes charges. For example, two EC2 instances in the same AZ usually exchange data at no charge, while moving traffic between AZs in the same region typically incurs a small fee. Cross-region transfers are significantly more expensive and should be avoided for high-volume flows. Another common source of egress is when instances access services via an Internet Gateway or NAT — traffic leaving the AWS network to the public internet can incur per-GB costs. Caching using CloudFront reduces origin pulls and therefore origin egress charges for public content. A common misconception is that cloud traffic is always cheap; in reality, seemingly small design choices, like placing database replicas in another region, can create large recurring bills. Takeaway: map your traffic flows, label high-volume paths, and prioritize co-location or caching before accepting cross-region or internet egress. Data Transfer Costs — Where and why they apply means minimize cross-az, cross-region, and internet egress by co-locating resources or using caching and private paths.. In practical terms, understand the billing boundaries that affect your architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

VPC Endpoints provide private, secure connectivity between your VPC and supported AWS services without traversing the public internet. There are two kinds you must know. Gateway endpoints are specific to S3 and DynamoDB. They act as a route table entry that directs traffic for those services to an internal gateway; importantly they are free to use, and they remove internet exposure for those service calls. Interface endpoints are powered by PrivateLink and create Elastic Network Interfaces with private IPs in your subnets. Use interface endpoints when a service supports PrivateLink or when you need private connectivity to many services such as SQS, SNS, Kinesis, or custom endpoints for your own services. A practical example: an EC2 worker in a private subnet that reads and writes lots of S3 data should use an S3 Gateway Endpoint to avoid egress charges. A frequent misconception is that interface endpoints are free; while they improve security they incur hourly and per-GB costs, so choose the endpoint type based on service and traffic volume. Final thought: design endpoints early for storage-heavy or chatty service traffic to avoid retrofitting expensive network paths.

When private instances need to initiate outbound internet connections, you have two main choices: a managed NAT Gateway or a self-managed NAT instance. NAT Gateway is a fully managed AWS service. It scales automatically within an Availability Zone and requires no OS-level maintenance. For production workloads where uptime and simplicity matter, a NAT Gateway is the preferred option despite per-hour and per-GB charges. A NAT instance, by contrast, is a regular EC2 instance running NAT software. It can be cheaper for extremely low-volume traffic and gives control over software and metrics, but it adds operational burden: you must handle patching, scaling, failover, and monitoring. For high-throughput or important services, the management overhead of NAT instances typically outweighs savings. A common misconception is that NAT instances always save money — if traffic volume grows, manual scaling and NAT instance failure can cause outages and hidden costs. Practical advice: estimate expected data processed through the NAT; if it is large or variable, choose NAT Gateway and focus on reducing traffic through private endpoints instead of relying on egress. NAT Gateway vs NAT Instance means nat gateway for reliability and low ops; nat instance for low-volume, tightly controlled scenarios where you accept management overhead.. In practical terms, trade-offs in cost, availability, and operational overhead. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS Global Accelerator provides two static Anycast IP addresses that serve as fixed entry points for your global users. User traffic goes to the closest AWS edge location by Anycast and then traverses the optimized AWS backbone to your application endpoints, such as load balancers or EC2 instances. This reduces latency compared with relying solely on the public internet and improves availability because Global Accelerator monitors endpoint health and fails over to the next healthy endpoint automatically. Use Global Accelerator when you have a global user base sensitive to latency or when consistent performance and quick failover are business requirements. A practical example: a web application with users across continents can route users to nearest edges and then across AWS network to the origin region, achieving large latency reduction. A common misconception is that Global Accelerator replaces CDN for static content; it does not cache content. Instead, pair CloudFront for caching with Global Accelerator for optimal routing of dynamic or TCP flows. Final question to reflect on: are your users globally distributed enough that round-trip time gains justify the service cost?

For IPv6-only subnets that require outbound internet access but must remain unreachable from the internet, the Egress-Only Internet Gateway is the proper tool. It functions like NAT for IPv6: it allows instances to initiate outbound connections while preventing inbound connections initiated from the internet. This preserves security for IPv6 resources that should not be publicly addressable while still enabling package updates or external A P I calls. A practical scenario: if you run IPv6-only compute that needs to fetch updates but must not accept inbound traffic, an Egress-Only Internet Gateway meets the requirement without resorting to IPv4 NAT. A common misconception is that traditional NAT Gateway covers IPv6; NAT Gateway is an IPv4 construct. The takeaway is to select the right mechanism for the IP family in use and to validate that route tables for IPv6 route outbound traffic through the egress-only gateway. Always verify endpoint reachability after configuration to ensure no unintended inbound exposure. Egress-Only Internet Gateway for IPv6 means egress-only internet gateway allows outbound ipv6 connections while preventing inbound internet initiation.. In practical terms, ipv6 outbound-only internet access without inbound reachability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now we'll step through the starter CLI commands that set up a NAT Gateway, update a private route table, and create an S3 Gateway Endpoint. Follow the commands as a sequence of discrete steps you can reproduce. First allocate an Elastic IP and create the NAT Gateway in your public subnet; the NAT Gateway requires the Elastic IP and will be assigned a resource ID. Remember to wait for the NAT Gateway to reach available state before creating routes. This sequence reproduces the scenario safely and is the baseline for validating both internet and S3 access from private instances.

Let's summarize the essential concepts you should carry forward. First, data transfer costs are driven by where traffic crosses billing boundaries: cross-AZ, cross-region, and internet egress are the common cost centers. Second, VPC Endpoints let you keep traffic private: use gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB to avoid egress, and interface endpoints for services supported by PrivateLink when private ENIs are appropriate. Third, choose NAT Gateway for production outbound needs because it reduces operational risk; use NAT instances only when traffic volumes are tiny and you accept the management overhead. Fourth, Global Accelerator is a performance tool: static Anycast IPs and AWS backbone routing reduce global latency and improve failover but do not cache content. Finally, use monitoring — VPC flow logs, CloudWatch, and Cost Explorer — to verify that your changes produce both functional and cost benefits. Apply these concepts together to balance cost, performance, and security in your network designs.

Keep three practical rules in mind. First: eliminate unnecessary egress by co-locating resources and using gateway endpoints for storage-heavy workloads. Second: prefer managed services like NAT Gateway for production to reduce operational overhead and hidden availability risk, reserving NAT instances only for tightly controlled low-throughput cases. Third: when you face global latency problems, consider Global Accelerator to route users over the AWS backbone using static Anycast IPs, and pair it with CloudFront for caching. These three rules lead to designs that are secure, performant, and cost-aware. Ask yourself which of these rules is most underused in your current environment and start there.
